explanations.answer: They will live and multiply and possess the land
explanations.explanation: Moses, Israel's leader, says obeying leads to this: “…so that you may live and multiply, and enter and possess the land that the LORD swore to give your fathers.” (Deuteronomy 8:1) Notice it's a promise attached to the commands, not just a pile of rules. Friend, that's a great deal.

explanations.answer: They will build a great temple for the LORD
explanations.explanation: No temple shows up in this verse. Moses says obeying leads to living, multiplying, and possessing the land the LORD swore to give their fathers. I love a big building project as much as the next stamper, but that's not on the list here.

explanations.answer: They will rule over every nation on the earth
explanations.explanation: That's a big jump, friend. Moses says they will live and multiply, then enter and possess the land the LORD swore to give their fathers. It's one land in this verse, not the whole map.

Moses says the LORD led them “…so that He might humble you and test you in order to know what was in your heart, whether or not you would keep His commandments.” (Deuteronomy 8:2) A test brings out what's really in there. I think that's like pulling a tray out of the oven to see how the dough actually turned out.

Moses doesn't use that word here. He says the LORD led them to humble them and test them in order to know what was in their heart. A reward is a prize at the end, and this verse is talking about the road itself.

Comfort isn't the word Moses picks in this verse. He says the LORD led them to humble them and test them, to know what was in their heart. Forty years in the wilderness doesn't sound like a cozy afternoon on the couch.

In their hunger, the LORD gave them manna to eat, which neither they nor their fathers had known. Picture waking up hungry and breakfast is something nobody in your family has ever seen before. That's a morning nobody forgets.

Honey does show up in this passage, but later, in the list of what the good land holds. The food in their hunger was manna, which neither they nor their fathers had known. Save the honey for the promised land.
Fish aren't mentioned anywhere in this passage. Moses says that in their hunger the LORD gave them manna to eat. It was food neither they nor their fathers had known.

explanations.answer: Every word from the mouth of the LORD
explanations.explanation: Moses says the manna was so they might understand that man does not live on bread alone, “but on every word that comes from the mouth of the LORD.” (Deuteronomy 8:3) Jesus answers the tempter with this teaching in the wilderness (Matthew 4:4). Bread keeps you going for a day, and the LORD's word is what you really live on.

explanations.answer: Whatever they can gather each morning
explanations.explanation: Gathering isn't what Moses points to here. He says people live on every word that comes from the mouth of the LORD. That's the lesson tucked inside the manna.

explanations.answer: The bread their fathers ate in Egypt
explanations.explanation: Egypt's bread isn't in this verse. Moses says the manna was something neither they nor their fathers had known, so it taught them something new. The lesson is that people live on every word that comes from the mouth of the LORD.

Moses says it plainly: “Your clothing did not wear out and your feet did not swell during these forty years.” (Deuteronomy 8:4) Forty years of walking, and the clothes held up. Friend, I've seen an apron give up after one batch of cinnamon dough.

Moses says the opposite of that. He says, “Your clothing did not wear out and your feet did not swell during these forty years.” (Deuteronomy 8:4) After forty years of walking, that's a lot of clothing staying put.

Moses says, “…just as a man disciplines his son, so the LORD your God disciplines you.” (Deuteronomy 8:5) It's a family picture. Proverbs 3:12 puts it as a father correcting a son he delights in. Everybody understands that one.
A servant isn't the picture Moses paints here. He says a man disciplines his son, and the LORD disciplines Israel the same way. That's a family picture, and it's a close one.
A neighbor is someone you wave at over the fence, friend. Moses picks a much closer person: a man and his son. The LORD disciplines Israel just as a man disciplines his son.

Moses calls it “a land of brooks and fountains and springs that flow through the valleys and hills.” (Deuteronomy 8:7) That's three kinds of water in one breath. After a wilderness described as thirsty and waterless, I think that sounds mighty fine.
Wells don't appear in this verse. Moses says brooks and fountains and springs flow through the valleys and hills. Those are water that's already moving, no digging mentioned.
Lakes aren't in this verse, and neither is rain. Moses names brooks and fountains and springs that flow through the valleys and hills. It's running water he's describing.

explanations.answer: They will eat without any scarcity
explanations.explanation: Moses says it's “a land where you will eat food without scarcity, where you will lack nothing.” (Deuteronomy 8:9) Lack nothing, friend. I've never once finished a batch and still had enough cookies.

explanations.answer: They will eat well only in good years
explanations.explanation: Moses doesn't hang any condition on it. He says they will eat food without scarcity and lack nothing. No catch about good years in this verse.

explanations.answer: They will eat what they trade for
explanations.explanation: Trading isn't mentioned in this verse. Moses says it's a land where they will eat food without scarcity, where they will lack nothing. That's the whole promise.

Close, but gold isn't the metal here. Moses says the land's rocks are iron and its hills are ready to be mined for copper. Gold does come up in verse 13, but there it's wealth that increases, not something mined.

Moses names iron and copper: “a land whose rocks are iron and whose hills are ready to be mined for copper.” (Deuteronomy 8:9) Gold does come up later, in verse 13, but as wealth that increases. This verse is about the ground, and the ground gives iron and copper.

explanations.answer: Bless the LORD for the land
explanations.explanation: Moses says, “When you eat and are satisfied, you are to bless the LORD your God for the good land that He has given you.” (Deuteronomy 8:10) Full belly, thank-you first. I'd say that's a good habit for any kitchen.
A seven-day rest isn't what Moses says here. He says that when they eat and are satisfied, they are to bless the LORD their God for the good land. Eating, then blessing.
Sharing with the nations isn't in this verse. Moses says when they eat and are satisfied, they are to bless the LORD their God for the good land He has given them. The blessing goes up to the LORD.

explanations.answer: When they are full and rich and settled
explanations.explanation: Moses warns, “Otherwise, when you eat and are satisfied, when you build fine houses in which to dwell, and when your herds and flocks grow large…” (Deuteronomy 8:12-13) Forgetting doesn't always show up with trouble. Sometimes it shows up with a nice house and a full pantry.

explanations.answer: When enemies surround them in battle
explanations.explanation: Battle isn't the time Moses points to here. He describes eating and being satisfied, building fine houses, and herds and flocks growing large. The warning is about the good times.

explanations.answer: When a famine strikes the land
explanations.explanation: Moses points the opposite way. He talks about when they eat and are satisfied, build fine houses, and see their herds and flocks grow large. The warning comes when things are going well.

Moses says, “…then your heart will become proud, and you will forget the LORD your God who brought you out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of slavery.” (Deuteronomy 8:14) Pride and forgetting go hand in hand there. A full house can leave less room for remembering.
Afraid isn't the word Moses uses. He says their heart will become proud, and then they will forget the LORD their God. Pride is the problem here, not fear.
Weary isn't what Moses says. After the wealth comes, he says their heart will become proud and they will forget the LORD their God. It's a heart that feels too big, not too tired.

Moses says the LORD their God is the One “who brought you out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of slavery.” (Deuteronomy 8:14) He puts that memory right next to the warning about forgetting. It's the very thing he doesn't want lost.
Moses really does say it. The LORD their God is the One “who brought you out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of slavery.” (Deuteronomy 8:14) That's exactly what he warns they could forget.
Moses says, “He brought you water from the rock of flint.” (Deuteronomy 8:15) Water from a rock, friend. I've tried squeezing a lot of things for results, and a rock was never on the list.
The Nile isn't named in this verse. Moses says the LORD brought them water from the rock of flint, in a thirsty and waterless land. The water came out of a rock.
A cloud isn't mentioned here. Moses says the LORD brought them water from the rock of flint. It's a very unlikely place to find a drink.

Moses says the humbling and testing were “…so that in the end He might cause you to prosper.” (Deuteronomy 8:16) The hard stretch had an ending in view. That's good news for anyone in the middle of a long wait.
Wander isn't the word here. Moses says the LORD humbled and tested them so that in the end He might cause them to prosper. The end of the road was meant to be good.
Moses doesn't say tremble. He says the humbling and testing were so that in the end the LORD might cause them to prosper. The goal was a good ending.

explanations.answer: My own strength made this wealth
explanations.explanation: Moses says, “You might say in your heart, ‘The power and strength of my hands have made this wealth for me.’” (Deuteronomy 8:17) That's the thought where you hand yourself the trophy. Right after, Moses steers them back to who really gives the power.

explanations.answer: Our fathers earned all of this
explanations.explanation: Moses doesn't mention the fathers earning anything here. The thought he names is, “The power and strength of my hands have made this wealth for me.” (Deuteronomy 8:17) It's a thought about my own hands.

explanations.answer: The land was always ours to keep
explanations.explanation: That thought isn't in this verse. Moses says they might say in their heart, “The power and strength of my hands have made this wealth for me.” (Deuteronomy 8:17) It's about their own strength.
Moses doesn't credit the land. He says, “…it is the LORD your God who gives you the power to gain wealth…” (Deuteronomy 8:18) The power comes from the LORD, not from the dirt.

Moses says, “…it is the LORD your God who gives you the power to gain wealth…” (Deuteronomy 8:18) So the power comes from the LORD, not from the land. I like a good rich piece of ground, but it doesn't get the credit here.

explanations.answer: To confirm His covenant with their fathers
explanations.explanation: Moses says the LORD gives the power to gain wealth “…in order to confirm His covenant that He swore to your fathers even to this day.” (Deuteronomy 8:18) It ties back to what He swore long ago. The wealth isn't random, and it isn't a trophy for them.

explanations.answer: To make the nations jealous of Israel
explanations.explanation: Jealous nations aren't in this verse. Moses says the LORD gives the power to gain wealth in order to confirm His covenant that He swore to their fathers. That's the reason the text gives.

explanations.answer: To pay for offerings at the tabernacle
explanations.explanation: Offerings aren't mentioned in this verse. Moses says the power to gain wealth is given in order to confirm His covenant that He swore to their fathers. That's the one reason he names.

This is a heavy one, friend. Moses says, “I testify against you today that you will surely perish.” (Deuteronomy 8:19) He says it about forgetting the LORD and going after other gods to worship and bow down to them. He's serious because the stakes are serious.

explanations.answer: They will wander forty more years
explanations.explanation: More wandering isn't what Moses says here. He testifies that if they forget the LORD and go after other gods, they will surely perish. It's a heavy warning, so I'd read it slowly.

explanations.answer: They will lose half of the land
explanations.explanation: Losing half the land isn't in this verse. Moses testifies that if they forget the LORD and go after other gods, they will surely perish. It's a serious line, and it stands on its own.

explanations.answer: The nations the LORD has destroyed before them
explanations.explanation: Moses says, “Like the nations that the LORD has destroyed before you, so you will perish if you do not obey the LORD your God.” (Deuteronomy 8:20) It's a sober comparison, and he means it. I think he wants Israel to hear it clearly.

explanations.answer: The people of Sodom and Gomorrah
explanations.explanation: Moses doesn't name Sodom and Gomorrah here. He says they will perish like the nations the LORD has destroyed before them, if they do not obey the LORD their God. It's a heavy line, so I'll stick to his words.

explanations.answer: The builders of the tower of Babel
explanations.explanation: Babel isn't mentioned in this verse. Moses compares them to the nations the LORD has destroyed before them. It's a heavy warning, and he says it plainly.
